restatements.text: Increases the penalty for assaulting an on-duty law enforcement officer from a maximum of one year in jail to a felony punishable by up to three years in prison.

findings.direction: increases maximum sentence lengths and reclassifies the offense as a felony
findings.quote: Assault on an on-duty law enforcement officer is a felony punishable by up to three years in prison.
findings.mechanism: It raises the maximum penalty from one year in jail to three years in prison.

analysis.answer: Current law makes assault punishable by up to one year in jail. This measure creates a specific, higher penalty for assaulting an on-duty law enforcement officer, classifying it as a felony punishable by up to three years in prison.
Incarceration costs will likely rise due to longer sentences. Because the offense becomes a felony, these costs will likely shift from county jails to the state prison system.

Taxpayers pay the increased cost of longer incarceration. Law enforcement officers may benefit if the higher penalty deters assaults. Individuals convicted of the offense bear the burden of longer sentences and the collateral consequences of a felony record.
Prosecutors may use the threat of a felony charge carrying up to three years in prison as leverage in plea negotiations.
The text addresses penalties for assaulting law enforcement officers by increasing the maximum sentence and reclassifying the crime as a felony.
Prosecutors gain discretion and leverage in charging and plea bargaining by having a heavier penalty available.

Whether longer sentences effectively deter crime is empirically disputed. Some research indicates that longer sentences reduce crime through deterrence and incapacitation, while other studies find they have a negligible deterrent effect and can increase the likelihood of future offending.
